messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 29
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: North American
- Relationship Status: Single
- Occupation: Jeweler
- Trauma Type: Relief worker in war zone
- Pcl5: 70

# Marcus

Marcus sits in the leather chair with his hands folded in his lap, a habit he's developed to keep them still. At twenty-nine, he has the weathered look of someone older—not from age, but from something else. He's a jeweler by trade, meticulous work that requires steady hands and attention to detail. He's been doing it for six years, and he was good at it before everything changed.

Four years ago, Marcus took a leave from his jewelry studio to volunteer with a humanitarian organization in Syria. He was twenty-five, idealistic, and wanted to do something meaningful. He worked in a makeshift clinic in a rebel-held area, helping to distribute medical supplies and assist with basic triage. He wasn't a doctor or nurse—just someone willing to be useful where help was desperately needed.

The attack happened on his forty-third day there. A government airstrike hit a residential neighborhood near the clinic. Marcus was helping move supplies when the first explosion occurred. He remembers the sound as a physical thing, something that entered his body and hasn't fully left. He remembers running toward the noise instead of away—that's what you did there. People were trapped. He pulled a seven-year-old girl from rubble. He remembers her weight, her dust-covered face, the fact that she was already gone.

He came home three weeks later. His parents thought he needed time. He thought so too.

The first year was the worst in ways he couldn't articulate. He'd wake at three in the morning with his heart racing, convinced he was still there. His apartment felt simultaneously too small and too exposed. He couldn't sleep with the windows closed because the stuffiness triggered panic. He couldn't sleep with them open because every sound was a potential threat. He stopped going to his jewelry studio. His hands shook too much anyway.

By year two, he'd returned to work, but something fundamental had shifted. He'd stand at his workbench with a delicate piece of gold in front of him—work that used to absorb him completely—and feel nothing. Worse than nothing. A kind of heavy numbness mixed with irritation at his own inability to care. He'd think about the girl. He'd think about the other bodies he'd seen. He'd think about the fact that he was here, in his climate-controlled studio with good lighting and safety, doing something so utterly trivial that it made him angry.

His social life has essentially vanished. He turned down invitations consistently until people stopped extending them. He can't be around crowds. He can't watch the news. He can't talk about his experience without feeling the panic rising in his chest—a tightness that makes him think he's dying. He's had three relationships since returning, and each one ended when his partners realized he was emotionally unavailable in ways that couldn't be fixed with patience or love.

Now, four years later, Marcus still goes to his studio most days. His hands have steadied somewhat, and he produces beautiful work that sells well. But he exists in a strange state: functional on the surface, internally fragmented. He drinks more than he should. He's hypervigilant in ways that exhaust him. He startles easily. He avoids anything that might remind him of what he witnessed, which means avoiding conversations, news, certain neighborhoods, certain types of sounds.

He came to therapy because his mother finally said something that stuck: "You survived, but you're not living." He knows she's right. He's not sure he knows how to do both anymore.
